entries.text: The authors propose a visual lip-reading system intended to preserve spatio-temporal information in lip video.
entries.condition: Lip-centered video frames are the input; sentence characters are the output.

entries.text: STFM is proposed to reduce feature dimensionality while retaining local spatial information.
entries.condition: Applied after the convolutional feature extractor and before the sequence model.
entries.quote: To fuse high-dimensional spatio-temporal features into low-dimensional temporal features while keeping the im- portant local spatial information, we propose a Spatio- Temporal Fusion Module (STFM), as shown in Figure 2.

entries.text: Temporal Focal blocks are proposed to capture short-range temporal dependencies; local self-attention is used for longer-range dependencies.
entries.condition: Convolutional encoder-decoder sequence model for lip-reading features.
entries.quote: We propose a novel convolutional block called Tem- poral Focal block (TF-block in short) to draw more atten- tion to short-range temporal dependencies within the neigh- boring frames.

entries.text: The authors claim their approach outperforms the then state-of-the-art on GRID and LRW and is comparable on LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: Authors' summary of results across the four named datasets; see Table 3 for WER values.
entries.quote: Our method achieves the state-of-the-art results on GRID and LRW datasets and comparable results with state-of-the-art approaches on LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED datasets using much less training data and training time.

entries.text: The abstract claims a 12-day training-time reduction attributed to the convolutional structure and local self-attention.
entries.condition: Abstract-level comparison; the comparator is not named in that sentence. Table 4 reports 19 days for TM-CTC, 22 days for TM-seq2seq, and 7 days for this method.
entries.quote: The training time is re- duced by 12 days due to the convolutional structure and the local self-attention mechanism.

entries.text: The authors state that their model is trained end-to-end and takes 7 days on LRS2 and LRS3.
entries.condition: Training on LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED; single GPU training is reported in Sec. 3.5 and Table 4.

entries.text: The visual front end uses two 3D convolution layers with kernel size 5, followed by ResNet-18.
entries.condition: Convolutional Feature Extractor configuration.

entries.text: STFM uses spatial pooling size n=5 and 512 output channels.
entries.condition: Implementation setting for STFM.
entries.quote: In STFM, the spatial size after Spa- tialPooling is set as n = 5 and the number of output chan- nels is set to 512.

entries.text: The encoder and decoder modules are stacked six times, and multi-head attention uses eight splits.
entries.condition: Implementation settings for the conv-seq2seq model.

entries.text: The convolutional feature extractor dropout rate is 0.5.
entries.condition: CFE implementation setting.

entries.text: The output character dictionary has 40 entries: 26 letters, 10 digits, one apostrophe, and three special tokens.
entries.condition: Decoder output dictionary D; [PAD], [EOS], and [SPACE] are the three special tokens.

entries.text: Training uses the prior ground-truth character sequence as decoder input to predict the next character.
entries.condition: Teacher-forced sequence training as described in Fig. 1; the output is character-level.

entries.text: Training uses Adam with default parameters and the learning-rate schedule cited to Vaswani et al.
entries.condition: End-to-end training; schedule uses model hidden size, step, factor, and warmupSteps.

entries.text: The learning-rate schedule factor is 1 on GRID and 0.1 on LRW, LRS2-BBC, and LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: Dataset-specific learning-rate schedule values.

entries.text: For LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED, curriculum learning begins with single-word examples and increases sequence length during training.
entries.condition: Curriculum strategy attributed to reference [11].

entries.text: The model is first trained on LRW and the LRS2/LRS3 pre-training sets, then fine-tuned separately on each corpus's train-val set.
entries.condition: The paper does not give the exact number of examples used at either stage.

entries.text: Training batch size is 50 for GRID/LRW and 12 for LRS2-BBC/LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: Dataset-specific training batch sizes.

entries.text: The model is ImageNet-pretrained and trained on one GeForce Titan X GPU with 12 GB memory.
entries.condition: Training hardware/pretraining reported in implementation details.

entries.text: Inference uses beam search with beam width 5.
entries.condition: Test phase; no language-model condition is given in this statement.
entries.quote: In the test phase, the beam search decoder is applied to the decoder and the beam width is set to 5.

entries.text: Evaluation uses word error rate, computed as substitutions plus deletions plus insertions divided by reference word count.
entries.condition: WER=(S+D+I)/NUM; reference/hypothesis normalization is not further specified.

entries.text: GRID is described as 34,000 sentences from 34 speakers, with 255 test utterances per speaker.
entries.unit: sentences; speakers; test utterances per speaker
entries.condition: Train, validation, and test sets are randomly divided; the paper does not say the split is speaker-disjoint.
entries.quote: The GRID dataset contains 34000 sen- tences uttered by 34 speakers.

entries.text: LRW contains 450,000 utterances, one word from a 500-word vocabulary per clip, with 29 frames over 1.16 seconds.
entries.condition: Dataset description; paper does not report the LRW test partition size or test-speaker count.

entries.text: LRS2-BBC is described as 143,000 utterances, over 2.3 million words, and a 41,000-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Dataset totals; exact train/validation/test counts and speaker counts are not reported here.

entries.text: LRS3-TED is described as about 150,000 utterances, over 4.2 million words, and a 51,000-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Dataset totals; exact train/validation/test counts and speaker counts are not reported here.

entries.text: Video preprocessing detects 68 facial landmarks, aligns using three points, crops 112×112 lip-centered images, and scales lip width to one-third of image width.
entries.unit: landmarks; alignment points; pixels; image-width fraction
entries.condition: Applied to all datasets; the three alignment points are the two outside-eye points and the middle lowest nose point.

entries.text: The authors evaluate on the test set of GRID, LRW, LRS2-BBC, and LRS3-TED using the corresponding trained model.
entries.condition: Evaluation datasets are explicit; exact test-set sizes/composition are incompletely stated for LRW/LRS2/LRS3.

entries.text: The authors report 1.7 and 0.7 lower WER points than prior best results on GRID and LRW, respectively.

entries.condition: Table 1 LRW WER values: TF-block-a 19.3 and TF-block-b 18.7.

entries.text: The authors report TF-block-b gains of 2.4%, 4.9%, and 5.3% against Transformer-seq2seq on LRW, LRS2-BBC, and LRS3-TED, respectively.

entries.text: Local self-attention wider than 100 positions is reported to match global self-attention accuracy; width 50 incurs a 0.8% accuracy drop.

questions.q: What are the method's main technical contributions?
questions.answer: It combines a spatially preserving STFM front end with Temporal Focal convolution blocks and local self-attention in a convolutional sequence-to-sequence lip reader.

questions.q: What exact benchmark results does the paper report, and what is known about their evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: The paper's Table 3 reports WER of 1.3 on GRID, 16.3 on LRW, 51.7 on LRS2-BBC, and 60.1 on LRS3-TED. It states test-set evaluation and beam width 5; split sizes are incomplete, and speaker/session overlap, seeds, external LM use, text normalization, and chance level are not reported.

questions.q: How comparable are the paper's state-of-the-art and training-efficiency claims?
questions.answer: The authors claim state-of-the-art WER on GRID/LRW and comparable LRS2/LRS3 results with less training data. They explicitly qualify cross-paper comparisons: MV-LRS was unavailable, their ablation baselines differ from results in [1], and single-GPU memory prevented end-to-end ResNet-50 training. Table 4 lists 10/19/22/7 training days and video-duration values without units. Their prose says a 2.4% TF-block-b gain on LRW, while Table 1 values imply a 3.4-point WER gap.

questions.q: Which evaluation or selection conditions remain unspecified?
questions.answer: Exact LRW/LRS2/LRS3 test-set composition, speaker/session overlap, run seeds and repetitions, validation-based model selection, pixel normalization, external language-model use, chance performance, WER text normalization, Table 4 duration units, and numerical warmup/total training-step settings are not given.

questions.q: Does the stated TF-block-b gain against Transformer-seq2seq agree with the ablation table?
questions.answer: Not for LRW: Sec. 4.2 states 2.4%, while Table 1's 22.1 and 18.7 WER values imply 3.4 percentage points (inference). The reported LRS2 and LRS3 gaps match the listed values.

questions.q: (writer) Do the Table 3 TM-CTC and TM-seq2seq rows on LRS2/LRS3 use an external language model in their source?
questions.answer: Yes: 54.7/66.3 and 48.3/58.9 are the +extLM columns of Afouras et al. Table 2; without LM the values are 65.0/74.7 and 49.8/59.9.

questions.q: (writer) Was any prior LRW result without word boundaries below 16.3% error?
questions.answer: Yes: Stafylakis et al. 2018 V16, 15.67% MCR without word boundaries (Table 6).

questions.q: (writer) Did earlier lip readers keep spatial layout instead of global average pooling?
questions.answer: Yes: Stafylakis and Tzimiropoulos 2017 and Stafylakis et al. 2018 replace average pooling by a fully connected layer; 3D-FPA applies a spatiotemporal pyramid attention mask.
Not named in the caption or Sec. 4.2.

questions.q: (triage) What does "not comparable" in Sec. 4.3 refer to?
questions.answer: The first attempt: ResNet-50 front end trained in two stages with LRS3 in place of MV-LRS(w); the final ResNet-18 end-to-end model (Table 3) is the one called comparable.
